results.title: 3Es
results.content_html:
We Need a Better Language for Development

The first public reflections on the 3ES Framework — Explore. Exploit. Execute.

Every field develops its own language.

Engineering has a language for precision. Finance has a language for investment. Project management has a language for delivery. Innovation has a language for creativity, experimentation and possibility.

Yet somewhere between innovation and execution, the language begins to disappear.

This is a place I have spent much of my professional life. A place where ideas are no longer vague, but not yet concrete. Where opportunities seem promising, but the evidence is still incomplete. Where organizations need to make significant decisions without pretending to have complete certainty.

Over time, I have become convinced that this space deserves far more attention than it receives.

We have become remarkably good at talking about how to generate ideas, and equally good at talking about how to deliver projects. The transition between those two worlds is often treated as if it happens naturally. In practice, it rarely does.

This article is my first attempt to describe that transition.

It is not a finished methodology, nor is it intended to compete with the many excellent frameworks that already exist. It is simply the first public expression of a way of thinking that has gradually emerged through conversations, projects and reflection.

For now, I call it 3ES.

Development begins long before a project exists

Many organizations unconsciously define development by the moment a project receives approval.

Once that happens, familiar structures take over. Budgets are established. Resources are assigned. Milestones are planned. Risks are documented. Governance begins to provide confidence that progress can be measured and managed.

There is nothing wrong with this. In fact, it is essential.

The difficulty is that the most consequential decisions have usually been made before any of those activities begin.

Long before someone creates a project plan, someone noticed a problem that others had accepted as normal. Someone observed a change in customer behaviour. Someone imagined a different future. Someone connected two seemingly unrelated ideas.

These moments rarely follow a structured process, yet they often determine the direction of everything that follows.

Development therefore does not begin with execution. It begins with curiosity.

The challenge is that curiosity alone is not enough. Eventually it must become understanding, understanding must become confidence, and confidence must become commitment.

Those are very different forms of work.

Three different conversations

The more I have worked with innovation, engineering and business development, the less I believe that development can be described as one continuous process.

Instead, I increasingly see three distinct conversations taking place.

The first conversation is about understanding.

The second is about believing.

The third is about building.

Each conversation asks different questions. Each requires different evidence. Each demands different ways of thinking. Trying to solve them all with the same methods often creates unnecessary frustration.

This is the thinking that led me towards what I currently describe as Explore, Exploit and Execute.

Not because three phases are somehow universally correct, but because they seem to reflect three fundamentally different purposes in the journey from uncertainty to value.

Explore is about understanding before deciding

Every meaningful development effort begins with uncertainty.

Not the uncertainty of whether something can be delivered, but the uncertainty of whether we are even looking in the right direction.

Explore is the deliberate decision to stay with that uncertainty a little longer.

Instead of rushing towards solutions, the purpose is to deepen our understanding of the situation itself. Problems become more important than answers. Observations become more valuable than opinions. Curiosity becomes more productive than certainty.

Ideas certainly emerge during this phase, but they are not conclusions. They are vehicles for learning. Each idea offers another perspective from which the problem can be viewed, challenged and refined.

Over time, patterns begin to appear.

Problems become clearer.

Connections become visible.

Possibilities begin to emerge.

Eventually the organization arrives at something that feels more substantial than an interesting idea. It arrives at an opportunity.

Not because every question has been answered, but because the opportunity appears worthy of deeper investigation.

Explore therefore does not produce projects.

It produces direction.

Exploit is where opportunities become investments

This is the part of development that I believe deserves far more attention.

I intentionally use the word Exploit, even though it may initially feel uncomfortable.

Here, exploitation is understood in its strategic sense: making the best possible use of something valuable.

The valuable asset is no longer simply an idea.

It is the understanding created during Explore.

Exploit is the discipline of treating that understanding seriously enough to challenge it.

This is where assumptions become explicit hypotheses. Rather than protecting our favourite ideas, we expose them to reality. We seek conversations that might prove us wrong. We build pretotypes that communicate intent before investing in complete solutions. We test value propositions before optimising products. We ask customers to react to possibilities rather than polished concepts.

The objective is not to remove uncertainty entirely. Development will always contain uncertainty.

The objective is to understand which uncertainties actually matter.

This is also where business begins to enter the conversation in a different way.

Questions about desirability, feasibility, viability and adaptability become central, not because they belong in separate frameworks, but because they describe different dimensions of the same opportunity.

Can people genuinely benefit from this?

Can we realistically create it?

Can it become a sustainable business?

Can it continue to evolve as the world inevitably changes?

At the same time, the opportunity must find its place within the organisation itself.

Does it strengthen our strategic direction?

Does it support our long-term vision?

Does it fit our capabilities, our ambitions and the markets we hope to serve?

These questions cannot be answered by one discipline alone.

Engineers, designers, commercial teams, leadership and customers each hold different parts of the truth.

Perhaps the most valuable outcome of Exploit is therefore not simply evidence.

It is shared understanding.

A common language that allows an organisation to make an informed decision together.

When Exploit reaches its natural conclusion, the organisation is no longer discussing whether an idea sounds exciting.

It is deciding whether the opportunity deserves investment.

Execute is still development

Execution is often presented as the point where uncertainty disappears.

I do not believe that is true.

Execution simply changes the nature of uncertainty.

The organisation has chosen a direction. It understands why the opportunity matters. It has gathered sufficient confidence to invest.

Now attention shifts towards creating value.

Traditional project management contributes enormously here. Planning, governance, stakeholder management and structured delivery remain essential capabilities.

Development projects, however, are different from delivery projects.

A development project still explores technical unknowns. It still learns from customers. It still discovers information that could fundamentally change the direction of the work.

Sometimes the greatest success is recognising that the original assumptions no longer hold.

Stopping is occasionally a better outcome than finishing.

Execution should therefore not be understood as following a predetermined path.

It is the disciplined pursuit of value while remaining willing to learn.

Three diamonds instead of one

One idea that continues to develop in my own thinking is that development may be better represented by three connected diamonds rather than one.

Each phase begins by opening possibilities before gradually converging towards a deliberate decision.

Explore expands understanding before identifying an opportunity.

Exploit expands knowledge before arriving at an investment decision.

Execute expands implementation before converging on realised value.

Each diamond serves a different purpose.

Each reduces a different kind of uncertainty.

Together they create a continuous movement from curiosity towards meaningful action.

A framework that will continue to evolve

I do not expect these ideas to remain exactly as they are today.

In many ways, that would contradict the very philosophy they attempt to describe.

Development is iterative.

Our understanding grows through application, conversation and reflection.

Frameworks should be allowed to mature in exactly the same way.

This article is therefore not a conclusion.

It is a starting point.

The first public expression of a framework that I hope will continue to evolve through practice rather than theory alone.

If 3ES eventually proves useful, I do not believe it will be because it introduces entirely new ideas.

I hope it will be because it helps us describe something that many practitioners already experience but struggle to articulate.

The space between innovation and execution has always existed.

Perhaps what has been missing is not another process.

Perhaps it has simply been a better language for development.

results.title: Rethinking the Space Between Systems
results.summary: Most organisations don’t lack systems — they lack connection between them. Reduce the hidden effort of navigating fragmented information.
results.content_html:
I have been presented with the software Orbit Online, and it made me reflect on something most organisations recognize but rarely articulate clearly:

Not in a dramatic way, but in a quiet, accumulated sense.

Work lives across Excel sheets, emails, specialised systems, and local structures that have all been created with good intentions. Each of them solves something. Each of them holds part of the truth. But taken together, they rarely form a complete picture.

So a significant part of the work becomes navigating between them. Finding the right version. Recreating context. Aligning information that already exists, just not in the same place.

A McKinsey study estimated that employees spend close to 20% of their time searching for internal information or tracking down colleagues for context. That number is worth sitting with. It says something about how much of our effort goes into handling fragmentation rather than moving work forward.

This is where Orbit becomes interesting to look at.

What it brings into focus is the idea of connectivity — not as a technical feature, but as a way of understanding work. Projects, resources, competences, communication, and documentation are not separate elements to manage individually.

Instead of asking organisations to move into a new system, it connects to what already exists and presents it in a way that makes relationships visible. You can follow the work across layers, move from overview to detail, and see how things are linked without having to reconstruct the story yourself.

It becomes less about where something is stored, and more about how it connects to everything else. And over time, that begins to reduce a type of effort that is rarely named but widely felt — the work of keeping systems aligned with reality.

If that effort can be reduced, even slightly, it opens up something else. A clearer overview of what is actually happening. A better sense of how resources and competences are being used. And the ability to move across data layers without losing context along the way.

Orbit is one way of approaching that.

Not as a finished answer, but as a perspective on how connected work might look when the system reflects the reality instead of sitting beside it.

If that line of thinking is relevant, I’m open to continuing the conversation — especially around how someone like Orbit Online supports that kind of overview, while still allowing you to drill into the details when it matters.

results.title: Collaboration Problem
results.summary: Innovation is no longer limited by ideas inside companies, but by our ability to collaborate across them. The real competitive advantage is shifting from better innovation processes to better collaboration models.
results.content_html:
For years, innovation has been treated as an internal discipline. Something to be organised, funded, and optimised within the boundaries of the firm. Boards ask for more ideas. Leadership teams invest in R&D. Organisations build innovation units, run workshops, and measure pipelines.

And yet, despite all this activity, progress often feels slower than it should.

Not because companies have stopped innovating. But because innovation has outgrown the company.

From firms to systems

There was a time when innovation could reasonably be contained. A strong internal team, access to capital, and proprietary knowledge were enough to create advantage. Companies could build, test, and scale within their own structures.

That logic is becoming less relevant.

Today, the problems worth solving rarely belong to a single industry. Energy is no longer just about energy. It is tied to digital infrastructure, regulation, and new consumption patterns. Healthcare depends as much on data systems and software as on medical expertise. Manufacturing is increasingly shaped by AI and connected systems. And sustainability, perhaps the most pressing challenge of all, cuts across everything.

In this landscape, no single organisation holds enough of the puzzle.

The European Commission’s 2024 report on innovation performance reflects this shift clearly. It points to innovation ecosystems—networks of companies, institutions, and public actors—as the primary drivers of innovation, rather than individual firms operating in isolation. Value is no longer created inside the firm and then pushed to market. It emerges between actors, through coordination, integration, and shared effort.

Technology accelerates this dynamic. Digital platforms connect industries that were once separate. AI systems depend on shared data and complementary capabilities. Complex systems require integration across domains. And speed leaves little room for sequential handovers between isolated players.

Innovation, in other words, has become a collective act.

The evidence is already there

This is not a speculative future. It is visible in the data.

Denmark offers a particularly clear example. The country consistently ranks among the strongest in Europe when it comes to research, knowledge production, and education. The foundation is solid. The ideas are there.

And yet, according to the OECD’s 2024 review, Denmark struggles to translate this strength into market impact. There is a persistent gap between what is known and what is realised.

It is tempting to interpret this as an innovation problem. But that would miss the point.

The challenge is not generating ideas. It is moving them across organisational boundaries and into execution.

Research published in 2024 by MDPI supports this view, showing that inter-industry collaboration significantly improves innovation performance, particularly in complex and technology-driven contexts. UNCTAD reaches a similar conclusion in its Technology and Innovation Report, arguing that cross-sector collaboration is not optional but essential if we are to address systemic challenges such as climate change and digital transformation.

The pattern is consistent across institutions: innovation happens more effectively when organisations work together.

We already know this.

What is less clear is why we struggle to act on it.

Organisations built for a different problem

The answer lies in how most companies are still designed.

Modern organisations are highly effective at internal optimisation. They create clarity around ownership, define incentives, establish governance structures, and measure performance with precision. This makes them efficient, scalable, and manageable.

But these same strengths become limitations when innovation moves beyond the firm.

Collaboration introduces a different kind of complexity—one that does not fit neatly into existing structures. Questions that are straightforward internally become ambiguous across organisations. Who owns the outcome? How is value shared? Who carries the risk? How do you align priorities when strategies diverge?

These are not technical questions. They are structural and relational.

And they are often avoided.

Instead, many companies resort to what might be called “safe collaboration”: partnerships that are limited in scope, innovation labs that sit at a distance from the core business, pilot projects that generate insight but rarely scale. The appearance of collaboration is there, but the underlying model remains unchanged.

The result is a familiar pattern. Strong ideas emerge, but they struggle to travel. Execution slows down. Momentum is lost somewhere between organisations.

In Denmark, this pattern is visible at a national level. A strong knowledge base coexists with challenges in commercialisation and scaling. The issue is not a lack of innovation capacity. It is the difficulty of connecting that capacity across actors.

A different kind of competition

If this diagnosis holds, it changes how we should think about innovation going forward.

For decades, innovation has been framed as a competition of ideas. The assumption has been that those who generate the best ideas will win.

Increasingly, that assumption looks incomplete.

The real competition is shifting towards something less visible but more decisive: the ability to collaborate across boundaries. To build structures that allow multiple organisations to work towards shared outcomes. To align incentives without relying on hierarchy. To create trust where there is no formal control.

This is not a small adjustment. It requires companies to rethink some of their most fundamental assumptions about control, ownership, and value creation.

It also requires patience. Collaboration, when done properly, is slower to start. It involves negotiation, alignment, and the building of relationships. But once it works, it creates a different kind of speed—the kind that allows ideas to move across systems and scale beyond what any single organisation could achieve alone.

In that sense, the winners of the next decade are unlikely to be those with the most advanced internal innovation processes. They will be those who are able to design and participate in effective ecosystems.

Not better ideas, but better collaboration models.

Beyond the firm

None of this suggests that companies should stop investing in internal innovation. But it does suggest that this is no longer enough.

The frontier has moved.

Innovation is no longer constrained by our ability to generate ideas. It is constrained by our ability to connect them. To integrate capabilities. To move from isolated efforts to coordinated action.

So perhaps the more useful question is not how to innovate more.

But how to collaborate better.

Because until we address that, innovation will continue to stall—not inside organisations, but in the space between them.

results.title: The Idea Gap
results.summary: How might we capture more ideas, before they disappear, and before we convince ourselves they’re not ready yet?
results.content_html:
Most organisations don’t have an idea problem. Spend a bit of time inside teams, projects, or even informal conversations, and it becomes obvious that people are constantly noticing things that could be improved. They see inefficiencies, missed opportunities, new directions. They connect dots between technologies, customers, and experiences. In many ways, ideas are everywhere.

The real problem sits somewhere else. Those thoughts rarely make it far enough to be worked on.

There is a small, almost invisible moment between having an idea and doing something with it. Not implementation. Not validation. Not building a business case. Just the act of getting it out of your head and into a form where it can be shaped, challenged, and developed.

If you look at how innovation is typically described, it is often visualised as a funnel. Many ideas enter at the top, and only a few make it all the way through to implementation. That part is well documented. Studies across industries often show that a large majority of new initiatives fail to deliver expected results, with estimates frequently pointing to 70–90% not meeting their original ambitions. The funnel is narrow by design.

But even that picture is incomplete. Because it assumes that ideas actually enter the funnel. Most don’t. They never make it out of people’s heads.

Strategyzer illustrates this clearly in The Invincible Company using venture capital data. Looking at early-stage investments, roughly 6 out of 10 lose money entirely, around 3 out of 10 deliver modest returns, and only a very small fraction generate outsized results. You cannot pick the winner in advance. You need idea volume, and you need to work with many options to uncover the few that matter.

At the same time, research from organisations like McKinsey points to another consistent pattern: even when strategies and ideas are defined, as many as 30–70% fail in execution. There is a persistent gap between thinking and doing.

Put those two observations together, and something becomes clear. We struggle both with getting ideas into the system and with carrying them through. But we tend to focus almost all our attention on the latter. In practice, the earlier problem is easier to miss.

People hesitate because the idea is not “ready”. They wait until it sounds smarter, clearer, more complete. Some capture it briefly, but never return to it. Others feel that if they cannot immediately explain the customer, the problem, and the value, then it is probably not worth pursuing.

The tools we typically use are not designed for this moment. A Business Model Canvas is powerful, but it assumes you already have something you can describe across customers, value, and revenue. Lean Canvas moves a bit earlier by focusing on problem and solution, but it still requires a level of clarity that early ideas rarely have. Most innovation frameworks, stage-gates, and governance models start from the same place: something that is already formed enough to be assessed.

Early ideas are not like that. They are incomplete, inconsistent, and often slightly irrational. That is exactly what makes them interesting.

Over time, different approaches have tried to get closer to this early stage. Rready’s Kickbox lowers the threshold and legitimises the messy beginning. Innovator’s DNA helps explain where ideas come from curiosity, questioning, connecting, but is less concrete when it comes to capturing them. Lean Canvas helps translate thinking into something more structured, once you are a bit further along.

And in many organisations, you see the same pattern repeat itself: people create their own simple formats. Idea cards. Opportunity cards. Quick prompts. Small ways of catching something before it disappears. That in itself says something.

We keep building tools to develop ideas, but the real friction sits earlier, in the transition from thought to something you can actually work with.

Part of this is structural. Most organisations are not designed to handle half-formed thinking. The formats we use expect clarity, logic, and direction. That is understandable, but it also means that early ideas have nowhere natural to go.

Part of it is psychological. We tend to overestimate how complete an idea needs to be before it is worth writing down. At the same time, we underestimate how much clarity only emerges after we start externalising it.

So we wait for the idea to become better before we give it a chance to become better.

The uncomfortable implication is that the quality of ideas is not only a function of how we develop them. It is also a function of how early we are willing to catch them.

Because if only a small fraction of ideas ever lead to meaningful outcomes, then losing ideas early is not neutral. It directly reduces your chances of finding the ones that matter.

And if many of the ideas that do enter the system still fail in execution, then the cost of never even starting is even higher than we tend to assume.

The question is not how to build better business cases. It is how to make it easier to take a vague thought seriously enough to put it down, and just structured enough to take the next step.

Because once something is on paper, it changes character. It becomes something you can react to. Adjust. Challenge. Share. It becomes something that can move.

Maybe that is where most innovation efforts quietly succeed or fail. Not in strategy. Not in execution. But in whether ideas ever make it across that small, invisible gap in the first place.

This is a starting point. Because if ideas never make it out of our heads, everything that follows becomes irrelevant.

results.title: The Idea Circle
results.summary: How might we become better at creating ideas by understanding what ideas are actually made of?
results.content_html:
Where do ideas come from?

Sometimes an idea arrives during a meeting. Sometimes while driving home. Sometimes halfway through a conversation or in the middle of a completely unrelated task. We often describe these moments as sparks of inspiration, as if ideas appear from nowhere and somehow choose us as their next destination.

Yet when I look back at ideas that have led to meaningful projects, changes, products, or improvements, they rarely seem to have appeared out of thin air.

More often, they seem to have emerged from a combination of things that were already there.

A problem that needed attention. A solution that became visible. An insight that connected pieces of knowledge. And occasionally an inspiration from somewhere entirely different.

Not as a process. Not as a formula. More as a way of understanding why some ideas emerge and others never do.

Most ideas begin with a problem, although we do not always recognise it as such. A problem can be obvious, like a customer frustration or a recurring operational challenge. It can also be subtle. A missed opportunity. A pattern that feels inefficient. A question nobody has answered yet.

The interesting part is that problems rarely exist alone.

When we spend time understanding them, they often reveal connections to other challenges. What initially looked like three separate problems may turn out to be symptoms of the same underlying issue. Equally, a single problem may be connected to customers, employees, processes, and strategy at the same time.

Instead of solving one isolated issue after another, we begin looking for solutions that create value in several places at once.

And that is where the second part of the circle enters.

Because when people hear the word solution, many immediately think of something new.

A new technology. A new platform. A new method. A new investment.

There is nothing wrong with new solutions. Many are valuable. Yet innovation has a habit of making novelty feel more attractive than familiarity.

The challenge is that every new solution arrives with its own baggage. New things require attention, learning, integration, maintenance, and trust. They solve problems while simultaneously introducing uncertainty.

What often gets overlooked is how many solutions already exist around us.

Organisations are full of underused capabilities, forgotten experiences, existing tools, and knowledge that has quietly faded into the background. Sometimes the most effective solution is not the newest one. It is the one we have failed to fully utilise.

The difference sounds small, but it can be significant. Improving something that already exists often creates momentum faster than introducing something entirely new.

Between problems and solutions sits what may be the most overlooked ingredient of all: insights. Not information. Insights. There is a difference.

Information is everywhere. Most organisations are surrounded by it. Reports, dashboards, project reviews, customer conversations, workshop notes, observations, and experiences are produced every day.

An insight appears when those pieces begin to connect.

When a customer comment suddenly explains a recurring operational issue. When a lesson from one project becomes relevant in another. When several observations point towards the same opportunity.

Insights are not created by collecting more information. They emerge when we create understanding.

This is why sharing knowledge matters. Why conversations matter. Why notes matter. Why reflection matters.

An organisation almost always knows more collectively than any individual inside it. The challenge is making that knowledge visible and useful.

Then there is inspiration. The part we talk about most. A book. A podcast. A conference. A customer visit. A conversation. An observation from another industry.

One of the most valuable skills in innovation is the ability to borrow perspectives from elsewhere. A hospital learns from aviation. A manufacturer learns from Formula 1. A software company learns from hospitality. New associations create new possibilities.

Yet inspiration feels different from the other ingredients. Sometimes we know exactly where it came from. Other times we do not.

An idea appears and we cannot trace the source. The connection seems to have formed somewhere below the surface, long before we became aware of it.

That is why I think of inspiration as the topping rather than the foundation. Useful. Powerful. Occasionally transformative.

But ideas can emerge without it.

Problems, solutions, and insights are harder to escape. Perhaps this is also why the Idea Circle never really stops turning. A new insight changes how we understand a problem. A problem reveals the need for a different solution. A solution generates new insights.

An unexpected source of inspiration connects elements that previously seemed unrelated.

The circle keeps moving.

And perhaps that is the real lesson.

Ideas are rarely isolated moments of creativity.

More often, they are the visible result of connections that were already forming beneath the surface.
